A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MatchFixAgent and provide readable text, algorithms, tables and figures. Inspection includes all 21 pages of v2 and all 24 pages of v3, including Appendices A–J. Relocated material can be reliably matched.

before.justification: v2 reports original translation-validation and repair experiments, manual disagreement analysis, model-adaptability experiments and ablations in Section 4.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds agreement auditing, disputed-case ablations, threshold experiments and Qwen-based evaluation.

M1.justification: The six semantic analyzers, test-generation/repair agent, verdict agent and 0.7 similarity thresholds remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–3 are reformatted without a substantive procedural revision. Appendix H explicitly presents potential optimizations as future work.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 2,219 translation pairs from 24 projects covering six programming-language pairs. v3's additional audits, threshold tests and Qwen evaluation use this retained coverage; they change sampling or configurations rather than datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: Oxidizer, AlphaTrans, Skel and RustRepoTrans remain the comparison methods. The standalone-agent and without-semantic-analysis ablations are retained. Testing the existing standalone agent on disputed cases extends its evaluation, while Qwen is another MatchFixAgent backend rather than a new competing method.

E3.justification: v3 adds evaluation of the standalone agent on 416 disputed cases and the 145 manually resolved cases, a manual audit of 110 agreed verdicts, and threshold experiments at 0.5, 0.7 and 0.9 using analyzer-versus-final-verdict confusion metrics. Appendix F also evaluates Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B across the full benchmark. These are substantial additional evaluation designs; the original settings remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's two component ablations and disagreement examples, v3 tests whether the standalone baseline handles disputed translations, audits errors shared by MatchFixAgent and existing tools, and studies threshold sensitivity. Appendices D.3, E and G add shared-error case studies, analyzer diagnostics and component-level cost analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the single-run limitation and provide no seed-based variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. v3's reviewer-agreement percentages extend the existing reviewer-consistency reporting rather than introduce a new uncertainty-estimation procedure. Testing different thresholds is not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The original validation and repair tables are numerically unchanged. v3 adds Qwen's 71.6% agreement rate, 106/110 correct agreed verdicts, and standalone-agent accuracies of 47.7% and 56.1% on the two manually resolved dispute subsets. Tables 3, 5 and 7 add development times, threshold results and component costs. Appendix D.1 also adds 83.7% reviewer agreement while retaining the unexplained 18.6% conflict figure.

T1.justification: The functional-equivalence definition and CFG/DFG similarity calculations are retained. Neither version supplies substantive theorem or proof developments. v3's confusion-matrix measures support an empirical analysis rather than introduce new mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain language-agnostic repository-level validation and repair, inexpensive language adaptation, and benefits from the multi-agent architecture. The headline validation, agreement and repair claims are retained. Shortening the abstract and conclusion does not materially change their scientific scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of performance on disputed cases, shared validation failures, threshold-dependent cost/correctness tradeoffs, open-model adaptability and practical optimization opportunities. Appendix G acknowledges unreliable cached-token reporting. These substantially extend the discussion, although Appendix I retains a statement denying equivalent-verdict checking that conflicts with the new audit in D.3.

D1.justification: v3 newly provides an artifact reference and states that implementation code, Docker images, human-study records, agent logs and trajectories are public. It adds pointers to prompts and reviewer comments, plus Qwen proxy, pricing and token-accounting details. v2 already documented runtime versions and logging, but lacked these substantial access and reproduction disclosures.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations including ReCodeAgent, CRUST-Bench, unsupervised programming-language translation and cross-language verification work. It removes the Agentless discussion and several general agent/SWE-bench references. The main positioning against existing validation techniques remains stable; publication and bibliographic updates are not new works.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: prior-work limitations, experimental setup, disagreement analysis and threats move into appendices. The abstract, overview and conclusion are condensed, explicit research-question framing and summary boxes are removed, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main-text layout and substantially relocates displays. The development-cost bar chart becomes Table 3 with an added time column; new Tables 5–7 present threshold, Qwen and component-cost results. Existing examples and prompt figures move to appendices, while the original result tables and ablation plots are retained and reformatted.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens evidence beyond v2's consensus-based ablation by testing disputed cases and auditing agreed verdicts. Open-model evaluation and explicit artifact disclosures also improve usefulness and reproducibility. The net gain is limited by reporting inconsistencies: Appendix I contradicts the new agreement audit, and Table 7 does not substantiate Appendix G's claimed 23.8-fold overall cost reduction.
